Maladaptive Strategies.value: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I have lost my connection to my community and culture

vignette: Tiana was twenty-two when the downtown arts center's blast doors sealed shut, trapping her inside as masked men paced the concrete floor, reading specific names from a torn notebook and compelling hostages to repeat coded political phrases. The heavy click of the locks, the forced discussions about her Pacific heritage, and the sheer inability to move became immediate triggers that rewired her nervous system. Whenever she hears a familiar name on the street or is drawn into that same restricted political dialogue at a community gathering, her body floods with the same suffocating terror she felt then, making her feel threatened by strangers even in ordinary situations. This sudden, visceral threat directly fractures her recollection of the event, yanking forward only the disconnected shards of the attack rather than a coherent timeline. Worse, each triggered wave of fear confirms her deepest convictions: that the perpetrators walked free while she was left to pick up the pieces, that her connection to her community and culture has fractured beyond repair, and that the art form she loved no longer holds any weight. Holding onto the belief that nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore directly pushes Tiana into rigid coping routines. She avoids enclosed spaces like rehearsal studios, forces herself to think only positive thoughts to silence the dread, and obsessively thinks about why the event has happened to her, searching for a logic that never emerges. Her conviction that accountability is impossible and that her cultural roots are severed directly pulls those memories further apart, leaving them even more disjointed and imageless. In turn, these entrenched negative appraisals make her hyper-vigilant to those same names and topics, ensuring the original triggers never fade. Because she feels the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, she interprets the lingering dread as proof that nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore and that no one will ever answer for what happened. Those sudden, imageless emotional surges act as internal triggers, causing her to instantly brace for the same names and restricted topics that first terrified her. The unprocessed, nonverbal nature of those memories directly drives her avoidance of confined spaces; because she cannot piece the event together, any locked door or crowded dressing room instantly feels like the arts center all over again. Meanwhile, the sudden recall of those trapped moments directly spikes her physiological alarm, keeping her constantly on high alert when she hears unexpected or loud sounds. Her constant, unrelenting threat monitoring directly amplifies her sensitivity to names and conversation topics, turning every familiar word into a fresh trigger. This relentless sense of danger drives her to avoid enclosed spaces and forces her to think only positive thoughts, as stepping into a hallway feels like inviting the attack back in. Forcing herself to think only positive thoughts while simultaneously avoiding confined spaces only deepens her perception that the world remains dangerously unpredictable, directly feeding her heightened threat sensitivity. Tiana's habit of demanding meaning from the unexplainable does nothing to quiet the event; instead, it strips away any chance of natural processing, leaving the fragmented memories more jagged and intrusive than before. Because she cannot integrate what happened, she doubles down on her belief that accountability will never come and that her cultural ties are permanently severed. Over the months, these loops calcified into habits that fractured her professional life. As a dancer, she can no longer navigate the mirrored rehearsal halls or the crowded backstage corridors, and she has stopped attending cultural festivals where the forced conversations would instantly collapse her composure. Her isolation is a protective wall she built because the community she once called her own feels like a place of contamination rather than refuge. She finally sought help after a solo rehearsal ended in panic when a colleague mentioned a similar historical event, realizing her body was still waiting for a door that will never open. Tiana is most afraid that the fragmentation will never resolve, but she is desperately hoping to reclaim the movement and cultural connection she thought was lost forever.
